dedupe_keys.name: resilience of six southeast us ports and the port cluster during hurricane matthew 2016

description: This study measured how six ports in the Southeast United States absorbed, adapted to and recovered from Hurricane Matthew in 2016, and whether the ports as a regional cluster were more resilient than each port alone. The researchers defined a quantitative resiliency measure, based on the NSF notion of absorbing, adapting and recovering, that follows system output through pre-event, absorption, disrupted, recovery and recovered states, and applied it to vessel arrival and dwell data of the ports of Miami, Everglades, Palm Beach, Jacksonville, Savannah and Charleston for 2016, derived from purchased AIS records and split into container, non-container cargo, tanker and passenger vessels. The work was done by Scott Parr (Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University) and Brian Wolshon (Louisiana State University) with student authors, for the Maritime Transportation Research and Education Center, a US DOT university transportation centre. Coverage is regional, across the Florida, Georgia and South Carolina coasts. The final report and the container arrival and dwell tables are free on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 (27 May 2020). Outcome: the region was more resilient than its individual ports, as one port recovered while another was disrupted, and the ports absorbed the storm poorly but adapted and recovered well. Limitations: the raw AIS data are commercial and not shared. The study illustrates post-event resilience analysis of maritime ports and relates to the USACE National Waterway Network catalogued here.
name: Resilience of six Southeast US ports and the port cluster during Hurricane Matthew (2016)
organisations: Maritime Transportation Research and Education Center (University of Arkansas)
outcomes: The port cluster was more resilient than its individual ports because ports entered disruption and recovery at different times; the ports absorbed the storm poorly but adapted and recovered strongly.
